articles.title: Osage Nation speeds up orphan well cleanup as federal oversight recedes
articles.content:
This story was originally published by Osage News, and is published through the Indigenous News Alliance.​

At the entrance to Harvest Land Farms, Fred Beartrack prepares to plug another orphaned well. Records indicated a cement plug covered it, but excavation and a casing cutout revealed no cement.

“There was no cement, so the data was wrong,” Beartrack of the Nation’s Department of Natural Resources, or DNR, said in a video posted to the Osage Nation’s Facebook page. The well was open down to 2,400 feet. Instead of a quick cap, the crew now has to clean the well out to the bottom and properly fill it with cement. Beartrack and his crew said this work could take anywhere from two days to two months.

“We don’t really know what’s down there,” he said. “People could have thrown anything in the well before we got here.”

To support our nonprofit environmental journalism, please consider disabling your ad-blocker to allow ads on Grist. Here's How

Beartrack said crews found only about a foot of cement at the top of the well, with nothing beneath it. They drilled past the freshwater zone and cemented the well from there up.

“That well is an example of everything that’s wrong,” he said, referring to how the DNR has battled inaccurate well data as it has plugged wells throughout the Nation’s reservation, which covers about 1,470,559 acres in northeastern Oklahoma.

When Osage News spoke with Beartrack, the Department of Natural Resources was at the end of Phase 1 of the Nation’s federally funded orphan well program. Beartrack said the agency has plugged about 160 wells since the program began, 70 to 80 of them this year. Crews have inspected at least 2,500 to 2,700 wells.

“We keep finding new wells every quarter section we get into,” he said. Many go back decades, to operators that disappeared or wells that were plugged to standards now considered inadequate. The pace of well plugging picked up after a significant change this spring.

To support our nonprofit environmental journalism, please consider disabling your ad-blocker to allow ads on Grist. Here's How

The Bureau of Indian Affairs’ Osage Agency used to approve every plugging permit the Nation filed. But on March 13, the Orphan Wells Plugging Office, or OWPO, revised its tribal grant guidelines for all Phase 1 and Phase 2 projects like the one Beartrack is working on.

The Bureau of Indian Affairs, or BIA, told the DNR that wells without a responsible party are not a federal function. That is a significant shift within the Osage Nation Reservation, where the BIA has long overseen oil and gas development as trustee of the Nation’s mineral estate, including drilling and plugging wells.

Adam Trumbly, superintendent for the Osage Agency in Pawhuska, said his office continues to review permits and issue well-plugging permits as appropriate.

“The BIA–Osage Agency is not issuing plugging permits for orphan wells plugged pursuant to the Department of the Interior’s Orphaned Wells Program Office Tribal Orphaned Wells Program,” Trumbly told Osage News in an email. “The Revised Tribal Grant Guidance removed the compliance requirements based on Section 7 of the Endangered Species Act and Section 106 of the National Historic Preservation Act.”

Trumbly said this revision reflects OWPO’s determination that tribal development and tribal implementation grants are “nondiscretionary” and that activities conducted under them are not “federal undertakings.”

He said this guidance means the Osage Nation no longer needs the BIA Osage Agency (or the Orphan Wells Plugging Office) to review orphan well plugging activities for Endangered Species Ace or National Historic Preservation Act compliance, and the BIA Osage Agency no longer has the authority to conduct those reviews.

The change follows a report that faulted the program’s slow start. Much of the blame stemmed from the Bureau’s lengthy permitting process. The criticism fits a longer pattern: Federal watchdogs have repeatedly faulted the BIA’s oversight of operators who work within the Osage Reservation.

Reporting by Grist and Osage News found roughly 2,300 documented orphaned wells in Osage, though the true number may be higher because many old wells were never recorded. Shane Brown / Grist / Osage News

Previously, the bureau reviewed each plugging application, verified the Department of Natural Resources’ photos and field data, then published a record of decision for a 30-day public comment period that often stretched to 45 days. Beartrack said the full process could take 120 to 130 days. Now, he said, it takes one to two weeks. The DNR still checks with the Osage Agency to confirm whether a well truly has no responsible party, whether leases were canceled or terminated, and how old they were.

“We ask the BIA almost daily questions,” Beartrack said.

The slowdown was a central theme of a February report from the Office of the Inspector General for the Interior Department. It found that as of December 31, 2024, the Osage Nation had plugged 14 of the 290 wells it planned for Phase 1, about 5 percent. The report cited delays in hiring a petroleum engineer, staffing shortages at the Osage Agency, and disagreements between the agency and the Nation over which permit applications qualified as emergencies.

As of January 30, the DNR had submitted 217 plugging permits since August of 2024. The Bureau of Indian Affairs had approved 90 of them. At a Natural Resources Committee meeting in March, Trumbly said the agency processed the permits as a courtesy and was working with a “skeleton crew” under a federal hiring freeze. Beartrack told Osage News that the agency had four or five people in the field to verify applications.

Adam Peltz, who works on orphan wells for the Environmental Defense Fund, or EDF, said tribal nations face hurdles that states don’t. Even if the Nation does the work well, it still needs the Bureau of Indian Affairs to review and approve its permits on time. “That part is out of Osage’s hands,” he said.

Peltz said the federal money itself is new. Until around 2020, he said, orphan wells were barely on the national radar. The bipartisan Regrow Act, passed as part of the 2021 Infrastructure Investment and Jobs Act, set aside $4.7 billion for well plugging by states, federal agencies, and tribes. It was the first federal funding of its kind. About $150 million went to tribes, with the Osage Nation receiving the largest share.

When the EDF built a national orphan well map a few years ago, Peltz said there wasn’t any data available for Osage County. He said many tribal nations and the federal Bureau of Land Management never prioritized oversight of oil and gas, while some states have their own agencies and databases. State records on old wells aren’t much better, he added: Oklahoma has about 18,000 documented orphan wells and is believed to have more than 300,000 undocumented ones, said Peltz.

Beartrack said the Osage Agency didn’t hand the program over to the Nation so much as step away. “They just said wells without a responsible party are not a federal function,” he said. “It’s not like they gave us carte blanche. They just said it’s not their problem. They kind of wash their hands of it more than anything else.”

That’s good for the program, he said, but it raises a bigger question for the Nation.

“What does that mean for the Osage Nation overall?” Beartrack said. “Are all of these orphan wells our responsibility? When they say that orphan wells are not a federal function, what does that mean?”

Beartrack said he believes Bureau of Indian Affairs leadership in Washington, D.C., made the decision, not the local agency. He said the bureau sent a formal letter announcing the change.

Former Principal Chief Geoffrey Standing Bear, now on the Osage Minerals Council, said he would like to see a scientific and environmental review for any federal action related to the change. The council has long argued that the BIA is the trustee of the Osage mineral estate.

The council focuses on attracting producers and leasing the mineral estate, while the Nation has kept the well plugging grant under the DNR. Peltz said the two goals shouldn’t conflict. Modern horizontal drilling in old fields only works if the old wells are plugged first, he said.

“Plugging old wells and developing new wells should not be in tension,” he said.

Before the change, much of the friction centered on what counted as an emergency. The Department of Natural Resources repeatedly flagged wells as emergencies; in March, Trumbly told committee members, “If everything’s an emergency, then nothing’s an emergency.”

Peltz said some states and tribes were filing almost nothing but emergency permits because it was the only way to break through the backlog. That isn’t how the system is supposed to work, he said. An emergency should be reserved for something like discovering a leaking well in someone’s backyard.

At the request of the Department of Natural Resources, the agency produced a weighted checklist. A score of 75 or higher for an actively leaking well or storage tank, high methane readings, or hydrogen sulfide near the wellhead marked a well as an emergency.

Beartrack said that the checklist never actually sped up permits. “It hasn’t changed any of the timing on how fast we get permits back,” he said.

A pumpjack in Osage County, where decades of oil and gas development have left the Osage Nation with a sprawling orphan-well cleanup.

Jim West / UCG / Universal Images Group via Getty Images

Peltz, who reviewed the checklist, said it closely resembles the scoring systems Texas and Louisiana use. An actively leaking well or storage tank threatens water and safety; high methane levels raise explosion risk; and hydrogen sulfide is among the most dangerous chemicals in the oil field. A measured fluid level above the deepest underground source of drinking water carries a weight of 50, below the threshold for an emergency. Peltz said that doesn’t prove groundwater is contaminated, but it is a risk factor worth checking.

“Could they have put that as a weight 75? Sure,” he said. “Is it a crime that they put it at 50? Not necessarily.”

The bigger problem, he said, is the scale. “The crime is that this was allowed to happen at this scale,” Peltz said, “and that it’s been so hard to work through it, even with the money flowing.”

The Department of Natural Resources still scores every well with it. Beartrack said some questions overlap or contradict each other. He has suggestions to fix them, but revising it isn’t a priority. “If it’s an emergency and the well has downhole conditions that would make it an emergency, then … we’re gonna plug it,” he said.

Beartrack said he is finishing contracts and purchase orders with rigs expected to roll in the next few weeks. Phase 2 has roughly 70 to 80 wells on deck to plug. He does not expect a dramatic jump in pace. “Maybe it should,” he said, “but … we’ll still be doing probably the same amount, 70 wells in this fiscal year.” The DNR’s field team is small, he said, and still has to gather and verify information for each well.

The Nation’s award comes to about $91 million over five years. Peltz said that won’t come close to covering Osage County, where no one knows how many orphan wells exist. Asked whether $91 million is enough, Peltz said, “No, not even close.”

Previous reporting by Grist and Osage News found roughly 2,300 documented orphaned wells in Osage, though the true number may be higher because many old wells were never recorded. Plugging a single well costs anywhere from $40,000 to $500,000, depending on its condition.

Peltz said the program needs the Nation to hire more engineers and procurement staff to get bids out, “hopefully to Osage Nation contractors.”

Asked whether oil drilling causes many of Osage County’s drinking water problems, Beartrack said, “Not if the wells are designed up to today’s standards.” That said, most of the wells his crews encounter are not. Many were drilled before operators routinely set surface casing deep enough to protect fresh water — something Beartrack said didn’t take hold until around the 1970s. Older wells, he said, “were OK for the standard of the day.”

At Harvest Land, the crew planned to finish the job the same way at every site: Clear the land, remediate it, and return it to its original surface, with the well capped and buried. “The final result is you won’t see anything,” Beartrack said. “And we’ll have a record of where it was.”

articles.personality_title: Osage Nation speeds up cleanup of old oil wells as federal oversight changes
articles.personality_presentation:
**Context** – The Osage Nation in northeastern Oklahoma has thousands of old, abandoned oil wells called orphan wells. These wells can be dangerous if not properly closed, risking water pollution and safety hazards. The federal government used to closely oversee the cleanup of these wells.

**What happened** – Recently, the Osage Nation’s Department of Natural Resources (DNR) has accelerated plugging these orphan wells. A rule change in March shifted federal oversight, allowing the Nation to handle more of the cleanup work directly without waiting for lengthy federal permits. Since the program began, the DNR has plugged about 160 wells and inspected thousands more. The change means permits now take one to two weeks instead of up to four months.

**Impact** – This faster process helps reduce environmental risks sooner across the Nation’s large reservation, which covers nearly 1.5 million acres. Many old wells were never properly closed and pose unknown dangers underground. By plugging them correctly, the Osage Nation protects groundwater and land, improving safety and health for their communities. The program is funded with about $91 million over five years, the largest share given to any tribe.

**What's next step** – The DNR plans to continue plugging around 70 to 80 wells each year. They are hiring more staff and preparing contracts for new equipment to keep the work moving. However, experts say the funding and resources still aren’t enough to cover all wells in the area. The Nation will also keep checking wells carefully to ensure they meet safety standards.

**One-sentence takeaway** – With new federal rules, the Osage Nation is speeding up the cleanup of dangerous abandoned oil wells, making their land and water safer for the future.
articles.personality_title_fr: La Nation Osage accélère le nettoyage des anciens puits de pétrole après un changement de supervision fédérale
articles.personality_presentation_fr:
**Contexte** – La Nation Osage, dans le nord-est de l’Oklahoma, compte des milliers d’anciens puits de pétrole abandonnés appelés puits orphelins. Ces puits peuvent être dangereux s’ils ne sont pas correctement fermés, risquant la pollution de l’eau et des dangers pour la sécurité. Le gouvernement fédéral supervisait auparavant de près leur nettoyage.

**Ce qui s’est passé** – Récemment, le Département des ressources naturelles (DNR) de la Nation Osage a accéléré le colmatage de ces puits orphelins. Un changement de règle en mars a modifié la supervision fédérale, permettant à la Nation de gérer directement davantage de travaux de nettoyage, sans attendre de longs permis fédéraux. Depuis le début du programme, le DNR a colmaté environ 160 puits et en a inspecté des milliers d’autres. Désormais, les permis prennent une à deux semaines au lieu de quatre mois.

**Impact** – Ce processus plus rapide permet de réduire plus tôt les risques environnementaux sur la grande réserve de la Nation, qui couvre près de 1,5 million d’acres. Beaucoup de vieux puits n’avaient jamais été correctement fermés et présentent des dangers inconnus sous terre. En les colmatant correctement, la Nation Osage protège les nappes phréatiques et les terres, améliorant la sécurité et la santé de ses communautés. Le programme est financé à hauteur d’environ 91 millions de dollars sur cinq ans, la plus grande part accordée à une tribu.

**Prochaines étapes** – Le DNR prévoit de continuer à colmater environ 70 à 80 puits chaque année. Il engage plus de personnel et prépare des contrats pour de nouveaux équipements afin de poursuivre les travaux. Cependant, des experts estiment que les ressources et financements restent insuffisants pour couvrir tous les puits dans la région. La Nation continuera également à vérifier attentivement les puits pour garantir leur sécurité.

**Résumé en une phrase** – Grâce à de nouvelles règles fédérales, la Nation Osage accélère le nettoyage des puits de pétrole abandonnés dangereux, rendant ses terres et ses eaux plus sûres pour l’avenir.
articles.personality_title_es: La Nación Osage acelera la limpieza de pozos petroleros abandonados tras cambio en supervisión federal
articles.personality_presentation_es:
**Contexto** – La Nación Osage, en el noreste de Oklahoma, tiene miles de pozos de petróleo antiguos y abandonados llamados pozos huérfanos. Estos pozos pueden ser peligrosos si no se cierran correctamente, causando contaminación del agua y riesgos para la seguridad. El gobierno federal solía supervisar de cerca la limpieza de estos pozos.

**Qué pasó** – Recientemente, el Departamento de Recursos Naturales (DNR) de la Nación Osage ha acelerado el tapado de estos pozos huérfanos. Un cambio en las reglas en marzo permitió que la Nación maneje más directamente la limpieza, sin esperar largos permisos federales. Desde que empezó el programa, el DNR ha tapado unos 160 pozos y ha inspeccionado miles más. Ahora los permisos tardan una o dos semanas en lugar de hasta cuatro meses.

**Impacto** – Este proceso más rápido ayuda a reducir los riesgos ambientales antes en la gran reserva de la Nación, que cubre cerca de 1,5 millones de acres. Muchos pozos viejos nunca se cerraron bien y pueden tener peligros desconocidos debajo. Al taparlos correctamente, la Nación Osage protege el agua subterránea y la tierra, mejorando la seguridad y salud de sus comunidades. El programa tiene un financiamiento de unos 91 millones de dólares en cinco años, la mayor parte para una tribu.

**Próximos pasos** – El DNR planea seguir tapando entre 70 y 80 pozos cada año. Están contratando más personal y preparando contratos para nuevo equipo para continuar el trabajo. La Nación también seguirá revisando bien cada pozo para asegurar que cumpla con los estándares de seguridad.

**Conclusión en una frase** – Con nuevas reglas federales, la Nación Osage está acelerando la limpieza de pozos petroleros abandonados peligrosos, haciendo que su tierra y agua sean más seguras para el futuro.

articles.title: How carbon credits helped unlock the Great Koala National Park in NSW
articles.summary:
BY THE OPTIMIST DAILY EDITORIAL TEAM The Great Koala National Park might sound like a place that’s too good to be true, but it is real. After more than a decade of campaigning, three state elections, and over 14 hours of parliamentary debate, New South Wales has established the state’s second-largest national park. It’s made […]
The post How carbon credits helped unlock the Great Koala National Park in NSW first appeared on The Optimist Daily: Making Solutions the News.
articles.content:
BY THE OPTIMIST DAILY EDITORIAL TEAM

The Great Koala National Park might sound like a place that’s too good to be true, but it is real. After more than a decade of campaigning, three state elections, and over 14 hours of parliamentary debate, New South Wales has established the state’s second-largest national park. It’s made up of 478,000 hectares (about 1.2 million acres) between Kempsey and Grafton on the Mid North Coast. More than 100 species of flora and fauna will be protected within its boundaries.

The park is a patchwork of existing protected areas stitched together with more than 178,000 hectares (roughly 440,000 acres) of former state forest and Crown Land. The legislation passed through approximately 160 amendments before it got there.

The campaign started small. Conservationist Ashley Love began lobbying for the park after hearing from local residents that koalas in the region weren’t as common as they once were. “It became too much to ignore,” he said. What started as a proposal to protect Crown Land eventually became a Labor election platform. NSW Labor took it to the 2015 and 2019 elections, lost both, and won government in 2023 on a ticket that included the park.

Carbon credits sealed the deal

Carbon credits were central to making the legislation work. The federal Clean Energy Regulator registered a project covering more than 117,000 hectares (about 289,000 acres) of the park’s state forest areas. By formally ending native forest logging there, the government can now sell carbon credits from the land. Protected forest, it turns out, generates more revenue than logged timber.

Of course, that trade-off still has real costs. The Forestry Corporation of NSW had already cut more than 30 jobs in Coffs Harbour as the logging moratorium ate into forward orders. Timber NSW president Andrew Hurford laid it out: “Staff have been laid off; engineering firms that provide support to those companies have no forward orders … downstream people supplying tyres, fuel, trucking, transport, engineering. All of those things are gradually becoming slower and quieter.” The government has committed to moving displaced Forestry Corporation staff into roles with the National Parks and Wildlife Service.

A park with gaps still to close

NSW Environment Minister Penny Sharpe called it “a defining moment for conservation in NSW,” and by the numbers, it qualifies. Love, whose decade of advocacy made the proposal viable, was more measured. “Its nature is quite fragmented, and there are gaps and connectivity issues between sections of it, but it is a big step forward,” he said.

Koalas need connected habitat to move, breed, and survive disease pressure. A 478,000-hectare patchwork is still a meaningful step up from what existed. The carbon credit structure gives the protected land a financial rationale that most past conservation campaigns lacked entirely. Love says he’ll keep pushing for the sections that didn’t make it in. After a decade, that sounds less like frustration than a habit he’s not planning to break.

The story provides detailed context on the campaign, legislative process, and economic trade-offs, highlighting a meaningful positive impact on biodiversity and climate action.
articles.personality_title: Carbon credits help create the Great Koala National Park in NSW
articles.personality_presentation:
**Context** – For many years, koalas in New South Wales (NSW), Australia, were becoming harder to find. Conservationists and local people wanted to protect the animals and their homes. After many years of effort, the NSW government worked to create a large new national park to help save koalas and other wildlife.

**What happened** – The Great Koala National Park was officially established after more than ten years of campaigning, three state elections, and long debates in parliament. It covers 478,000 hectares (about 1.2 million acres) between the towns of Kempsey and Grafton. The park combines existing protected areas with former state forests and Crown Land. A key part of making this happen was using carbon credits, which allowed the government to earn money by protecting forests instead of cutting down trees.

**Impact** – This park is now the second-largest national park in NSW and will protect over 100 types of plants and animals. Using carbon credits to fund protection is new and important because it shows that saving forests can be more valuable than logging them. This helps fight climate change by keeping trees standing, which absorb carbon dioxide. However, some jobs in logging were lost, so the government plans to help those workers find new roles in park services.

**What's next step** – Although the park is large, it is made up of different separate areas that need to be better connected for koalas to move and live safely. Conservationists plan to continue working to fill these gaps and expand protection. The success of using carbon credits may encourage similar projects in other places.

**One-sentence takeaway** – By using carbon credits to protect forests, NSW has created a huge new national park that helps koalas and other wildlife while supporting climate efforts.

articles.title: Louisiana’s accidental blueprint for restoring its coast
articles.content:
This coverage is made possible through a partnership between Grist and Verite News, a nonprofit news organization with a mission to produce in-depth journalism in underserved communities in the New Orleans area. ​ ​​​ ​ ​​​

Arthur Matherne is used to speeding his airboat across a southeastern stretch of the Louisiana coast where lakes and bayous have widened as the Gulf of Mexico’s salty water has moved in, dissolving marshes and swamps.

But in one tucked-away patch of the Barataria Basin’s 1.6 million acres, the semi-retired tour guide eases off the throttle as he tries to remember his way through channels that have grown tighter by the year. Grasses are overtaking the shallows, and oak branches are spreading overhead, dangling Spanish moss over waterways he once barreled through.

“All this, it’s filling in,” Matherne said after shutting off his airboat’s roaring propeller. “Right here, it used to be three feet of water. Now it’s three inches.”

What Matherne is seeing is a striking reversal of a pattern that has defined south Louisiana for the past century. While much of the coastal zone has receded at about 11 square miles per year from erosion and other forces compounded by climate change, the wetlands here are gaining ground.

To support our nonprofit environmental journalism, please consider disabling your ad-blocker to allow ads on Grist. Here's How

The reason is just a few miles away. Near Luling in St. Charles Parish, the Davis Pond Freshwater Diversion has funneled Mississippi River water into the basin since the U.S. Army Corps of Engineers built it in 2002 to combat saltwater intrusion. But something unexpected happened. The diversion also carried the muddy river’s sediment into the wetlands, raising the bottom and helping create new land.

“It’s had this unintended consequence of building land,” said Jacob Berkowitz, an Army Corps of Engineers wetland scientist. “This became one of the strategies that’s considered a key to addressing coastal land loss in Louisiana.”

U.S. Army Corps of Engineers scientist Jacob Berkowitz discusses the growth of wetlands south of the Davis Pond Freshwater Diversion. Tristan Baurick / Verite News

Yet even as Davis Pond demonstrates the land-building potential of river diversions, Louisiana has abandoned its most ambitious attempt to put that approach to work. Last year, the state canceled the massive Mid-Barataria Sediment Diversion, a $3 billion project inspired by Davis Pond and once heralded by the state as “the largest and boldest environmental restoration project in U.S. history.” Though it broke ground in 2023, work stopped shortly after Governor Jeff Landry, a Republican and one of the diversion’s most prominent critics, took office in 2024. He officially terminated the project, which would have been located 20 miles south of New Orleans, in July 2025.

Landry called the diversion a costly and ineffective “experiment” that would harm the commercial fishing industry by flooding parts of Barataria Bay with too much freshwater and sediment, pushing out shrimp and burying oysters.

To support our nonprofit environmental journalism, please consider disabling your ad-blocker to allow ads on Grist. Here's How

“This project is going to break our culture,” Landry told state lawmakers in 2024. “It will destroy the shrimping industry – which is already struggling – and destroy the oyster beds.”

Landry’s administration also canceled a companion project – the $1.8 billion Mid-Breton Sediment Diversion, aimed at reviving dying wetlands southeast of New Orleans.

Despite Landry’s opposition to these projects, his administration is quietly planning more diversions along the Mississippi, albeit on a smaller scale.

Officials with the Louisiana Coastal Protection and Restoration Authority declined to discuss the state’s diversion plans, but a Verite News review of the authority’s budget documents indicates the state plans to spend at least $340 million on five projects over the next several years that would divert Mississippi River water to restore coastal wetlands. That represents a big increase over past spending on diversions. Since 2007, CPRA has completed just three diversion projects totaling $47 million, according to the agency’s 2027 annual plan.

While some state leaders may disparage diversions, CPRA scientists still believe using river water to rebuild land and restore wetlands is a sound approach. At its core, a diversion mimics how the Mississippi functioned before levees walled off its floodplain, preventing the river from overflowing its banks or breaking through them at points called crevasses, according to Brian Gossman, a CPRA coastal scientist, speaking during a public lecture in March.

“The natural process that we’re attempting to harness is the Delta cycle,” Gossman said. “It’s the same process that built all of coastal Louisiana over millennia. We’re just using it in a targeted way.”

An airboat travels through a canal south of the Davis Pond Freshwater Diversion in Louisiana. Water and sediment from the diversion has helped build land and increased the growth of wetland trees and grasses. Tristan Baurick / Verite News

Nearly all of the authority’s diversion spending would go to one project — the restoration of Maurepas Swamp, a Chicago-sized wetland along the west edge of Lake Pontchartrain, about 25 miles from New Orleans.

The $334 million project, which broke ground in 2024, will install gates in the Mississippi River levee near Garyville in St. John the Baptist Parish and channel up to 2,000 cubic feet per second of water into Maurepas, which remains one of the country’s largest swamps despite losing thousands of acres of cypress and tupelo forest. Levees built in the early 1900s cut the swamp off from freshwater and sediment, leaving its trees vulnerable to saltwater intrusion.

According to the CPRA, the diversion will rebuild lost land and flush out stagnant, salty water, rejuvenating about 45,000 acres. It’s set for completion late next year.

The authority hasn’t totally given up on diverting sediment into the Barataria Basin. After canceling the Mid-Barataria Sediment Diversion, the agency dusted off an earlier, much smaller version of the project: the Medium Diversion at Myrtle Grove. Proposed more than 25 years ago, the project would divert up to 15,000 cubic feet of river water per second into the basin — about one-third of Mid-Barataria’s typical operating rate. To speed up the creation of marsh, the authority would also dredge sediment from the Mississippi and pump it directly into the basin.

The Myrtle Grove project’s timeline and budget are unclear. CPRA’s budget documents indicate about $1.7 million could be spent on it between 2027 and 2029, but the full cost will likely be much more. In 2012, the project was estimated at $278 million, or about $480 million in today’s dollars.

CPRA’s spending plans would also boost the Davis Pond diversion. The agency has proposed spending $3 million, shared with the Army Corps, to study how the diversion could be operated to build more land.

Research led by Tulane University in 2019 suggested that boosting the diversion’s average flow from 1,000 cubic feet per second to between 4,000 and 7,000 cubic feet per second could deliver more sediment to nearby wetlands. But if the flow is too high, researchers warned, the sediment will be flushed away.

In St. Charles Parish, home to Davis Pond, finding ways to increase the diversion’s flows has strong support. In its 2025 habitat restoration plan, the parish endorsed the proposed CPRA study, citing criticism that the diversion’s operations were “not being aggressive enough” to maximize its benefits.

Matherne stands on a platform used by scientists to track the growth of new land created by the Davis Pond Freshwater Sediment Diversion. The semi-retired tour guide says the wetlands south of the diversion are expanding, and wildlife is thriving. Tristan Baurick / Verite News

Watching Davis Pond’s silty flows creep past his airboat, Matherne agreed the diversion should release more water and sediment. “Right now, it’s like pissing in an Olympic-size swimming pool,” he said. “We need more flow.”

The Army Corps built the diversion to improve oyster beds that had become too salty as coastal marshes receded. Oyster abundance in the area has fluctuated since the diversion was built, but recent monitoring data suggests populations on public beds were above their 10-year averages in 2024, according to Danielle Richardi, a CPRA coastal scientist. Shrimp catches south of the diversion hit a nearly four-decade high that same year, she said.

Matherne said he’s seen a marked increase in wildlife. Alligators are more plentiful, he said, pointing out more than a dozen of the reptiles as his boat traveled the maze of waterways near the diversion. “All the alligators you see – that’s a fraction of what’s out there,” he said. “Come back at night, and you’ll see their eyes shining all over.”

Several studies have documented how accumulated sediment has built land near the diversion, although researchers in recent years have reached conflicting conclusions about the overall impact on wetland acreage.

In 2019, Louisiana State University coastal sciences professor Eugene Turner challenged conventional thinking about river diversions with a study linking Davis Pond to increased wetland loss. Turner found that the annual rate of wetland loss near Davis Pond nearly tripled after the diversion began operating, increasing from 0.36 percent to more than 1 percent. The increase was greater than in nearby wetlands unaffected by the diversion.

One explanation might have to do with what’s in the water. While the diversion was intended to restore the Mississippi’s pre-levee connections to surrounding wetlands, the river’s water has changed dramatically over the past century. It now carries high concentrations of nitrogen and phosphorus, much of it from fertilizer and manure runoff from farms and wastewater discharged by cities upstream. Turner argues that the excess nutrients produce wetland plants that are, essentially, flabby and weak.

“If your garden is fertilized too much, it puts all its growth aboveground,” he said. “It falls over because its roots never had to work hard.”

Turner believes that lower nutrient levels encourage plants to develop stronger root systems, making marshes more resistant to erosion. He likens some of the apparent land gains from diversions to a “green toupee.” The wetlands may look as though they’re filling in, but strong winds or currents can easily strip away the vegetation.

Two of Turner’s colleagues disputed his findings in a 2023 study. John White and John Day, also LSU coastal sciences professors, found that the first 20 years of Davis Pond’s operations had actually led to a net gain of 1.3 square miles of land. Their study said Turner came to an “erroneous conclusion” by incorrectly using data “that was clearly labeled as inappropriate for the task.”

The researchers asserted that Turner’s satellite data were too imprecise to distinguish small patches of wetlands from open water, potentially making land appear to have disappeared when it hadn’t.

Turner stands by his findings, arguing they more accurately portray how diversions affect coastal wetlands and warn of the damage they can cause if poorly managed.

Opponents of the Mid-Barataria diversion regularly cited Turner’s research and added several more concerns, including the CPRA’s projections that the huge diversion could bury oyster beds under sediment and that added freshwater would likely push shrimp farther offshore, making them harder to catch. Combined with the project’s $3 billion price tag, those concerns cratered political support.

“Considering the uncertainties and questionable environmental outcomes recognized by various agencies … it was necessary to abandon the current project,” CPRA Chairman Gordon Dove wrote in a column in The Times Picayune.

Although the CPRA has yet to fully explain its new approach to diversions, smaller and cheaper projects appear to be a priority. Turner welcomes that shift, but argues diversions should also operate at lower flows to avoid washing away vegetation that he believes excessive nutrients have weakened. He also recommends building diversions in areas with sandy soils rather than the soft, unstable soil in many marshes.

“It’s not that they won’t work,” Turner said. “These diversions give you lessons. We should learn from them.”

articles.personality_title: Louisiana’s river water projects help wetlands grow despite challenges
articles.personality_presentation:
**Context** – Louisiana’s coast has been shrinking for decades because of erosion, saltwater from the Gulf of Mexico, and climate change. Wetlands like marshes and swamps are disappearing, causing problems for wildlife and nearby communities.

**What happened** – Since 2002, a project called the Davis Pond Freshwater Diversion has been sending freshwater and sediment from the Mississippi River into part of the Barataria Basin. This has unexpectedly helped build new land and restore wetlands. Although a bigger project to do this on a larger scale was canceled in 2025, the state is still planning several smaller projects to use river water to protect and grow wetlands.

**Impact** – The Davis Pond project shows that using river water and sediment can help wetlands grow, which is important because wetlands protect against storms, support wildlife like shrimp and oysters, and prevent land loss. In some areas, wildlife such as alligators has increased, and shrimp catches reached a high point. This approach mimics how the Mississippi River naturally built land before levees blocked its flow.

**What’s next step** – Louisiana is moving forward with a $334 million project to restore the Maurepas Swamp by diverting river water to it. Smaller projects like the Myrtle Grove Diversion are also planned. Scientists continue to study how to best operate these diversions to maximize land growth while protecting local industries like fishing.

**One-sentence takeaway** – Using Mississippi River water to rebuild Louisiana’s wetlands is showing promising results and remains a key strategy despite political and environmental challenges.

articles.title: Scientists begin tests on human composting, an eco-friendly alternative to burials and cremation
articles.summary: Humans have caused irreversible changes to our planet in their time on Earth, pollution that continues even in death. Cremation relies heavily on fossil fuels, while traditional burials take up land. So is there a more eco-friendly way to honour our loved ones? French scientists are exploring the possibility of composting human bodies, a process that returns those who have died to the earth. Our Down to Earth team reports.
articles.content:
Video content Program Environment

Scientists begin tests on human composting, an eco-friendly alternative to burials and cremation

From the show

Reading time 1 min

Humans have caused irreversible changes to our planet in their time on Earth, pollution that continues even in death. Cremation relies heavily on fossil fuels, while traditional burials take up land. So is there a more eco-friendly way to honour our loved ones? French scientists are exploring the possibility of composting human bodies, a process that returns those who have died to the earth. Our Down to Earth team reports.
articles.reasoning: The article reports on a scientific initiative to develop human composting as an eco-friendly alternative to traditional burial and cremation methods, which have significant environmental impacts. This represents a meaningful environmental innovation with broad societal relevance and potential to reduce pollution and land use associated with death care practices.
articles.personality_title: French scientists test human composting as a green alternative to burial and cremation
articles.personality_presentation:
**Context** – Traditional ways of handling bodies after death, like burial and cremation, affect the environment. Burials use up land, and cremation burns fossil fuels, which pollute the air.

**What happened** – Scientists in France have started experiments to see if human composting can be a safe and eco-friendly option. This process turns human bodies into nutrient-rich soil, helping return them to the earth naturally.

**Impact** – If successful, this method could reduce pollution and save land space that burials usually take. It offers a new way to respect those who have passed away while caring for the planet.

**What's next step** – Researchers will continue testing to ensure the process is safe and effective. If approved, human composting could become an option for people in the future.

**One-sentence takeaway** – French scientists are exploring human composting as a natural and earth-friendly way to handle bodies after death, aiming to reduce environmental harm.
articles.personality_title_fr: Des scientifiques français testent le compostage humain comme alternative écologique aux enterrements et crémations
articles.personality_presentation_fr:
**Contexte** – Les méthodes traditionnelles pour gérer les corps après la mort, comme l’enterrement et la crémation, ont un impact sur l’environnement. Les enterrements utilisent de l’espace, et la crémation brûle des combustibles fossiles qui polluent l’air.

**Ce qui s’est passé** – Des scientifiques en France ont commencé des expériences pour voir si le compostage humain peut être une option sûre et écologique. Ce procédé transforme les corps en un sol riche en nutriments, aidant à les rendre à la terre naturellement.

**Impact** – Si cela réussit, cette méthode pourrait réduire la pollution et économiser l’espace utilisé par les enterrements. Elle offre une nouvelle façon de respecter les défunts tout en prenant soin de la planète.

**Prochaine étape** – Les chercheurs vont continuer à tester pour garantir que le procédé est sûr et efficace. Si c’est approuvé, le compostage humain pourrait devenir une option pour l’avenir.

**Résumé en une phrase** – Des scientifiques français explorent le compostage humain comme moyen naturel et écologique de gérer les corps après la mort, pour réduire les dommages environnementaux.
articles.personality_title_es: Científicos franceses prueban el compostaje humano como alternativa ecológica a entierros y cremaciones
articles.personality_presentation_es:
**Contexto** – Las formas tradicionales de manejar cuerpos después de la muerte, como el entierro y la cremación, afectan al medio ambiente. Los entierros ocupan tierra, y la cremación quema combustibles fósiles que contaminan el aire.

**Qué pasó** – Científicos en Francia han comenzado a experimentar para ver si el compostaje humano puede ser una opción segura y ecológica. Este proceso convierte los cuerpos en un suelo rico en nutrientes, ayudando a devolverlos a la tierra de forma natural.

**Impacto** – Si tiene éxito, este método podría reducir la contaminación y ahorrar espacio que normalmente ocupan los entierros. Ofrece una nueva manera de honrar a los fallecidos mientras se cuida el planeta.

**Próximo paso** – Los investigadores seguirán probando para asegurar que el proceso sea seguro y efectivo. Si se aprueba, el compostaje humano podría ser una opción en el futuro.

**Resumen en una frase** – Científicos franceses están explorando el compostaje humano como una forma natural y amigable con la tierra para manejar cuerpos tras la muerte, buscando reducir el daño ambiental.
